Thirty interest groups and individuals appeared before our Legislative Committee, and about 100 amendments were proposed. Half of these were accepted. We therefore believe this is a fair and equitable report that takes into consideration the proposals submitted by the witnesses who appeared before the Committee and by Committee members who were most diligent in their work and in attending the Committee's proceedings. The result is that a stronger and more comprehensive Bill can now be reported back to the House.

In closing I would like to say that acting as chairman for the committee has been an enriching experience for me personally, and I would like to take this moment to thank all the staff of the Members, the House of Commons and the Library, who made the work of the committee flow so smoothly.

subsubtopic: POSTAL DELIVERY SERVICE TO NEW RESIDENTIAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, pursuant to Standing Order 106, a petition organized by Mr. Ed Tchorzewski (MLA for Regina North East) and signed by the residents of Park Ridge in the City of Regina. These residents pay taxes and pay the same price for postage as anyone else, but do not receive the service of door-to-door mail delivery. Canada Post's policy of not extending mail delivery to new residential districts means that the people who reside in Park Ridge, Regina, will receive less consideration than residents in more established communities.
Therefore, this petition of 196 citizens of Park Ridge are praying and calling upon the House of Commons to initiate a change in Canada Post's policy so that mail delivery services will be provided to those neighbourhoods that meet delivery criteria.

On the Order: Government Orders
Consideration of an Opposition Motion-
That this House urges that the Government press upon the Government of the United States the unanimous views of the House of Commons as expressed in its resolution of May 23, 1986, and insist that the United States rescind the 35 per cent duties on British Columbia cedar shakes and shingles and guarantee that similar measures or other possible trade action will not be applied to Canadian products in the future if the present comprehensive trade negotiations are to proceed.-Mr. Tobin.
By consent, the motion is moved by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I so move.
May 27, 1986

I want to thank the House for the unanimous consent in allowing me to appear on behalf of the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) who will be following me in the course of the debate. I want to congratulate that Member from Newfoundland, who represents a very heavy forest industry in his riding, for having brought this to the attention of the House with such despatch.
The issue that absorbs us this morning and throughout the day concerns double-dealing by the President of the United States and the American Government because the imposition of a 35 per cent tariff against British Columbia red cedar shingles and shakes offends the very spirit and runs contrary to the very thrust of the current free trade negotiations between our country and the United States. The imposition of the tariff ran directly counter to the efforts of two Governments to enhance our respective access into each other's markets. In fact, as it affects B.C. red cedar and, indeed, the entire lumber industry, we already have a free trade arrangement that is now being offended rudely by a 35 per cent tariff. I might say that this tariff is so severe that at 35 per cent it is in effect a barrier that prohibits the entry of B.C. shingles and shakes to the American market.
This double-dealing also reflects the incompetence of the Government in the handling of our negotiations with the United States. We now have a situation where the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) have no compass, no sense of direction and no sense of purpose. On the two occasions of the so-called Shamrock Summits with the President-where the only winner was St. Patrick and certainly not the people of Canada-the Prime Minister boasted of his special relationship with the President. He boasted of a closer relationship that he was fashioning between our two countries. Yet the President, the Prime Minister's partner, friend and confident, the man that he said was only on the other end of the telephone, was the one who used his presidential discretion and imposed this 35 per cent tariff on B.C. red cedar.
That special relationship was replaced by bombastic rhetoric, by promises of retaliation and by threats from the Prime Minister as he escalated his vocabulary to feign outrage and turn on his erstwhile partner. We have something to say about that because we will prove in the House that the Prime Minister was not surprised and had received full warning from the Premier of British Columbia well in advance of the presidential action.
The negotiations have been handled very badly. Prior to sitting down with the United States, the Prime Minister had already thrown away the Foreign Investment Review Agency, thrown away the National Energy Program and thrown away the book publishing industry. He had already received a weak commitment on acid rain and the President had made a unilateral deal with the U.S. Senators on our Canadian lumber industry in order to get free trade on the fast track.
Not only have the cards been thrown away, the timing for beginning the negotiatons was lousy. We have a $20 billion
Supply
surplus with the United States. The average American Congressman thought that his or her real problem was Japan with its $50 billion surplus. Now they are looking directly at us and analysing our trade. This will not be a philosophical discussion with the United States, but a hard-nosed, eyeball-to-eyeball negotiation. The Americans will look at every item and every number and their objective in these trade negotiations will be to reduce our surplus of $20 billion down to zero. That is what they are trying to do with the shakes and shingles. That is what they are trying to do with lumber and fish. That is why they would like to reopen the Auto Pact. That is the message we are getting now from the President of the United States.
Of course, the negotiations were undertaken on the false premise, as we have heard from many of our independent institutes across the country, that the very fact of negotiating a trade arrangement with the United States would dissipate protectionist pressure in the U.S. Congress. That is a naive assumption. These negotiations seem to have done just the opposite. Focusing the attention of the American Congress on Canadian trade has perhaps even exacerbated those protectionist instincts or, at least, rather than being vaguely focused around the world against Japan or Europe, they have been focused on Canada as well.
We do not know how to respond to this issue from day to day. I am going to make a statement in another forum on the whole free trade subject. We set forth fully our position on September 26, when I spoke before Your Honour for an hour in the House of Commons. Our caucus met on January 19 when we again set out our position which carries the unanimous support of our caucus. We will further define that position when we assess the situation. However, we have not seen any facts.

There has been no clarification, no education of the public, no parliamentary debate to give Members of all parties a chance to contribute their insights, reflexions and opinions and those of their constituents. Not a single opportunity was given. Even the documentation provided by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) was censored. Every single page, and there were even a few pages missing entirely, every single page had been doctored prior to producing the documentation, so that Canadians are unable to judge the pros and cons, the advantages and liabilities, the cost and benefits of a future agreement. And provincial participation is practically nonexistent. There is some confusion here. What do the words "full provincial participation" mean? The Premier of Ontario doesn't know, the Premier of Quebec doesn't know, the Premier of British Columbia doesn't know. These talks are being pursued in an amateurish, clandestine and absolutely incompetent fashion.

Our negotiators' lack of understanding of the American position has been absolutely negligent. Apparently we were

May 27, 1986
Supply
taken by surprise by the close vote and the opinions of the 20 U.S. Senators on the Finance Committee of the United States Senate. What was our embassy doing? What was the 100 person trade office, set up under Mr. Reisman, doing here in Ottawa? Why were we taken by surprise?
I suggest that the Government should not have been surprised about this issue as well. I am holding a copy of a letter to the Prime Minister of Canada from the Premier of British Columbia, the Hon. W. R. Bennett. It is dated May 7, 1986.1 will read it into the record:
My dear Prime Minister:
As you know an investigation has been conducted under Section 201 of the U.S. Trade Laws regarding imports of wood shingles and shakes from Canada. The International Trade Commission has determined injury to U.S. industry and has forwarded recommendations to President Reagan.
The Commission is divided in its recommendations with one-half recommending no restrictions and the remaining three Commissioners recommending a 35 per cent tariff be applied.
The matter now rests with the President who has full discretion in deciding what action, if any, is to be followed. He is required to announce his decision on or before May 24, 1986.
I am deeply concerned that the President may in fact decide to impose a tariff, perhaps for extraneous reasons.
He may decide to show that he is not reluctant to act on Section 201 cases. Furthermore, in view of the difficulties surrounding the Senate Finance Committee decision to provide the President with fast track authority, he may decide to demonstrate a tough posture vis-a-vis Canada.
This matter is of great importance to Canada and, in particular, to British Columbia. The jobs of an estimated 4,000 workers across Canada are threatened. I urge you to contact the President directly so as to convince him not to act in any way against Canadian shingle and shake imports into the U.S.
The final two paragraphs merely reinforce that particular argument and the letter is signed by the Premier of British Columbia.
In other words, the Prime Minister was warned directly by the Premier of the province most intimately affected. He was urged to contact the President of the United States. We do not know what was done. We suspect nothing was done. Yet despite this knowledge, the Prime Minister feigned surprise and outrage. It was a phoney reaction. It was a manufactured reaction and cosmetic bombast. The Prime Minister knew about the issue. He should not have been surprised. He had been warned by the Premier of British Columbia.
We have a very serious situation in British Columbia involving the B.C. cedar industry. I met yesterday in my constituency office with a committee representing the entire lumber industry of British Columbia. It told me that this tariff has the following direct job and dollar effect on the Canadian economy; first, the loss of 4,000 direct jobs with an annual payroll in excess of $100 million; second, raw materials suppliers face the loss of revenues in excess of $100 million; third, transportation loss of revenues resulting in approximately $55 million; four, suppliers to the industry face losses in excess of $25 million; five, financial institutions face losses of revenues of $36 million on short-term financing, not to
mention the long-term financing and the problem now facing the whole industry in terms of the availability and continuance of credit. These direct effects total more than $344 million per year. That is concentrated in B.C. cedar and the shingles and shakes industry, because white cedar was excluded, and related industries, which are directly involved. With respect to the indirect dollar effect, the industry representatives made the point very well.
The irony of the situation is that the action taken by the President is not going to help the American shake and shingle industry because it faces, as do our Canadian suppliers, a declining North American market. Cedar used to represent a considerable percentage of roofing in North America. It is now down to 3 per cent because of the competition of asphalt and tile. This will leave the American industry crippled because it is now going to be without raw material to manufacture its part of the industry. Moreover, it is going to be absolutely captive to the big lumber and logging companies of the United States, the Weyerhaeusers, the Georgia Pacifies, the Boise Cascades. It will now not have any competitive counterweight against the tremendous economic power it faces. The President's action will not help the American industry but it will absolutely cripple, even destroy, our lumber industry in British Columbia because at 35 per cent we do not have a tariff, we have a wall which cannot be climbed.
Is this a shot across the bow of the Canadian lumber industry? Is this a harbinger of things to come? The Canadian lumber industry has become a pawn in the trade discussions with the United States. I have already recited the letter from the President of the United States to the senior Republican Senator of the State of Oregon, Senator Packwood, Chairman of the Finance Committee of the U.S. Senate which piloted that fast track resolution. He is also the senior senator from the largest forest-producing state in the Union. He received a separate deal. That deal was consecrated in a letter we put before the House from the President to the senator saying to him, and to other senators, we suspect: "Don't worry, boys, about these free trade negotiations with Canada because the lumber negotiations will be kept separate and I, as President, will enforce the full weight of the American law to protect our lumber industry". And that is what has happened.
Now a countervail action has been filed by the American industry against our Canadian industry, not only in British Columbia but in New Brunswick, Ontario, Newfoundland, Quebec and right across the board. The law has not changed. Our industry won a countervail action in 1983. The facts have not changed. But perhaps there is connivance on the part of the administration that this time a countervailing action will succeed. The President still has until June 6 to use his discretion as to whether or not he will receive that petition from the American industry. If the President refuses the petition, the action does not go any further. If he receives the petition, the whole quasi judicial process in the United States proceeds inexorably towards some kind of conclusion. Of course, the Canadian industry suspects the worse. It suspects
May 27, 1986

that the attitude of the United States' administration has changed adversely against Canadian interests.
Our position on this issue can be summarized in this way. First, we want the Prime Minister to call the President of the United States directly on the telephone, use the advantages of that vaunted special relationship with the President and accept the President's invitation to call him any time he has a problem. We want him to ask the President two things. We want him to ask the President to reverse the 35 per cent duty on B.C. shingles and shakes and to exercise his discretion to refuse the countervail petition of the American lumber industry against the Canadian lumber industry. We want our Prime Minister to suggest to the President that while trade negotiations are continuing between our two countries, we negotiate with the United States-and it can be done simply by an exchange of letters between the President and our Prime Minister-a standstill agreement or what I have called a "cease and desist" agreement, so while any general discussion on trade are being taken between our two countries the unilateral harassment actions like the imposition of tariffs or countervailing actions on both sides of the border cease and desist.
If we do not get a satisfactory response from the President on these issues then, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) suggested in the House at the end of last week, we as a country should seriously consider reassessing these negotiations with the United States on trade, or suspend them until we get some understanding of what is going to happen by way of the unilateral harassment actions.
We do not believe that this is the time for retaliation. We believe this is a time for cool assessment by our Canadian Governments. This is a time for negotiation and a time for ascertaining the real mind of the President and of his administration. I am supported in that view by the President of the IWA, Jack Munro. I am supported in that view by the Premier of the Province of British Columbia with whom I spoke on Sunday. I am supported in that view by the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia with whom I met yesterday, and I am supported in that view, I understand, by the Member of Parliament for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain), the chairman of the Conservative caucus. That is the attitude we ought to take, not this sort of catch up ball which the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) are trying to play in order to make them look tough after they have looked like patsies for the last year and a half. It is not going to work.
Finally, we want a statement from the Government that if the tariff persists there is adjustment for our industry and for our workers in British Columbia who have been been put absolutely out of business.
I know exactly what I am doing here, and if the Government had known what it was doing we would not have had to put this motion forward. That is our position. We look forward with great interest to what the Government will propose. We
Supply
look forward with great interest to see how the Prime Minister responds. This issue could have been foreseen. It was highlighted to the Prime Minister. It was signalled to him by the Premier of British Columbia. Any feigned surprise will not wash. Any phoney, bombastic, cosmetic rhetoric just will not fly. We present this motion to the House with the utmost conviction and the utmost sense of outrage at the futile conduct of the Government throughout this whole matter.
Hear, hear!
Are there questions or comments? The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain).

Mr. Speaker, in a spirit of resolving a situation which is very traumatic and dramatic for western Canada, I appreciate the concern that all individuals and all Hon. Members have taken with respect to this issue that deals with an acute situation that has arisen, especially in my riding.
I have a couple of questions to ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition. He alluded to the fact that this is an inappropriate time to commence free trade talks because of the $20 billion imbalance. What is the position of the Liberal Party? Does it have a position as a Party? Why has it not enunciated it before now? We have been listening.
Are you deaf?

I say to Hon. Members that we will not stand in our places and say that we will not listen to other people. We have maintained from the very beginning that we will consult and conciliate with every Canadian in seeking a resolve to some of the major problems which face the country, especially in terms of improving the plight of Canadians who seek jobs. My first question is, will the Hon. Member deary enunciate the position of the Liberal Party? The Hon. Member says that this is an inappropriate time. I would like him to respond to the 300 protectionist Bills which are sitting in the Congress and in the Senate of the United States. Does he feel that they will just disappear or that some fairy godmother will come down and strike these things off the face of the earth? I would like him to respond to those questions if he could, please. I would like the tone of this debate to be positive so that we can all work toward a resolve.

Mr. Speaker, I can understand the embarrassment which the Hon. Member feels. I sympathize with his constituents since they are very deeply affected by this issue. We are trying to find a solution.
First, the position of the Liberal Party was set forth in a one-hour speech I made on September 26 in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister introduced the resolution in a short, vague and ambiguous speech which took 15 minutes, and we have not heard from him since in the House of Commons.

May 27, 1986
Supply
Second, he can find our position in a caucus statement dated January 19 which carries the full force of our caucus. It was distributed to the House and to the media. It sets forth our position. I believe I will have an opportunity to render that even more precisely before the House rises.
I am saying that the position of the Opposition has been very clearly set forth. Our problem is, as it is the country's, that we do not know where the Government stands. There has been no statement of principles. There have been no facts which set it forth. We have not been told what is negotiable and what is not. We have not been told what is on the table and what is not. The provinces are in the dark. The Canadian public has no facts at all.
We believe the timing was bad because a $20 billion surplus is not the best opening gambit. Nor is it good timing to begin negotiations in an election year when key U.S. Senators and key U.S. Congressmen will not be able to look at this issue with the type of objectivity which one would expect and hope in a free trade arrangement.
In terms of the protectionist sentiment in the United States, the naivite of the Government was and remains, I suppose, that beginning negotiations would dissipate that protectionist sentiment in the U.S. Congress and those 200 Bills would just disappear. That has not turned out to be the case. My response to the Hon. Member is, what price does he want the country to pay to dissipate that protectionism? We are looking constructively at the discussions. We have laid out what we believe are the benchmarks. However, the negotiations have been handled so ineptly that the country is shaken to its roots by the incompetence of the Government.
Hear, hear!

Mr Speaker, I have two short questions to which I hope the Hon. Member will respond. Yesterday, when he met with the same group with which I met, he indicated that it was his position, and I assume the group thought that it was the position of his Party, that he wanted to have the comprehensive trade talks suspended until the 35 per cent duty in relation to shakes and shingles was removed. That is not what the motion suggests. I wonder whether you could clarify if that is your position that is, if the 35 per cent duty placed against shakes and shingles is not removed then you want those talks to terminate.
The second question is in relation to log and bolt exports to the United States. Mr. Clark is on the record as opposing the movement of any cedar logs or bolts-

Order, please. The Hon. Member is starting to use "you" again. I remind him that questions are directed through the Chair. I think he knows he should also refer to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I wonder if the Hon. Member could expand with respect to what is the position of the Liberal Party in relation to the log and bolt exports.

Mr. Speaker, when I met with the representatives of the shake and shingle industry I expressed our view exactly as I have expressed it this morning. First, we want the Prime Minister to test the President and the President's willingness to withdraw the tariff against B.C. red cedar shakes and shingles. Second, we want the Prime Minister to test the President as to whether or not he will exercise his discretion and refuse the petition on countervail against the Canadian lumber industry. Third, we want to know whether he would agree to some sort of cease and desist or standstill agreement with Canada while the negotiations are proceeding. Failing that, we would have to consider reassessing or suspending our free trade negotiations with the Americans. That was my position then and that is my position now. Let us stay with shakes and shinges and we will deal with the other matter on another occasion.
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has said that he opposes retaliations which would trigger a trade war.
So did you!

I oppose any action that would trigger a trade war. If the Hon. Member's position is one in which he seeks a solution to this problem, does he have a definitive position? I go back to this question because the Liberal Party should have a clearly enunciated position and it does not seem to have one.
Where have you been?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Wake up, you've been sleeping too long.
Bye-bye, Gerry.
Order, please. The Hon. Member knows that I have to allow time for a reply. Will he complete his question or comment briefly, please.
They said bye-bye in 1983 and 1984 and I proved them wrong then, and I will prove them wrong again.
You didn't have shakes and shingles hanging around your neck then.

The Hon. Member wants the Government's position which, without question, has been clearly enunciated. I ask him for the position of the Official Opposition. He says that he gave the position in a speech and that he clarified it further as he went along. I say this in sincerity. We want as much constructive criticism or as many constructive points as can be brought forward in this debate. It is an issue critical to British Columbia and to all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Hon. Member that he ought to review what I said in the House on September 26. He ought to review our caucus statement as well. He ought to bring both documents into his own caucus
May 27, 1986

and ask the Prime Minister where he stands on all the issues we have outlined before the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Second, we will be as constructive as we can. On behalf of our caucus I believe I have put forward a very constructive proposal to the House this morning. I hope the Hon. Member will reinforce it through the very eminent position he holds in the caucus of the Conservative Party.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate. I would like to begin by taking a close look at the motion before us. In my view, it does not address what has taken place; it wanders, and I think it is worth reading. It is as follows:
That this House urges that the Government press upon the Government of the United States the unanimous views of the House of Commons as expressed in its resolution of May 23, 1986-
The motion reads very well up to that point. It refers to the motion introduced by the Leader of my Party and unanimously supported by the House on Friday. The motion then goes on to read as follows:
-and insist that the United States rescind the 35 per cent duties on British Columbia cedar shakes and shingles-
It reads well to that point. However, it then goes on to say the following:
-and guarantee that similar measures or other possible trade action will not be applied to Candian products in the future if the present comprehensive trade negotiations are to proceed.
That is about as vague as one could possible word the tail-end of a motion. It basically means that the Liberal Party is not calling for a suspension of the trade talks at this time because Liberal Members do not view this as being a matter substantive enough to have those talks suspended.
I think we have to look at what the House did. We have to be very careful and methodical about how we will get the 35 per cent duty removed. I learned yesterday that the President has not yet signed that duty into law. The announcement was made by the White House, but there is still a vague opening. There is still an opportunity for us to remove the 35 per cent duty.
How do we go about removing the duty? The Cabinet is meeting today to look at placing retaliatory duties against oranges, for example, or products from Washington, Oregon, Idaho, northern California and other areas. We must ask ourselves how the U.S. administration will respond if those kinds of tariffs and duties are placed against their products. That will pound the final nails into the coffin of this issue. There is no way either Reagan or the U.S. administration will back off once those kinds of retaliatory measures begin.
I would encourage Members of the House to take some time to read about what happened in the late 1920s and on into
Supply
1930 when the Smoot-Hawley Bill was introduced in the United States and kicked off a trade war that had effects all the way around the world. Part of what precipitated the Smoot-Hawley process and the trade war was Canadian wood products. It is an extremely sensitive area and we have to look carefully at what has been said so far because we are beginning to see the personality of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) revealed.
We heard the statements made by the Prime Minister here in the House on Friday. As the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) has pointed out, the Prime Minister knew for three weeks that this was being precipitated. We knew that Paula Stearn, the Chairperson of the International Trade Commission Secretariat that looked at the shake and shingle issue, voted with the other two members of the commission that there be no countervailing duty brought against B.C. shakes and shingles, but the other three members of the commission voted for it. Then the President stepped in and here we have to deal with the whole question of good-faith negotiations between the President and Canada.
It is clear that there was not a clear launch to the negotiations. I will deal with that more extensively in few moments. Time and again, the Prime Minister has said that we have to give the benefit of the doubt in most of these situations to the President of the United States. Anyone who has ever played cards knows that the first time someone is caught cheating at cards, very tough action has to be taken because that person will continue to cheat while playing cards if he finds out he can get away with it.
The American administration managed to pillory a $250-billion B.C. industry without a peep from the Premier of British Columbia. He has not asked that the talks be suspended. He is waving in the wind on retaliatory action. The Prime Minister used the harshest words used in this century against the President of the United States but, so far as I have been able to learn today from people here in Ottawa, he has not had a response to that telex. There has not been a response to Mr. Clark's initiative with Mr. Shultz, nor has there been a response to any External Affairs or embassy initiatives.
We have here a very clear example of bad faith on the part of the President of the United States. I think we have to look back with care to earlier this month and recall the note scribbled on the bottom of the letter written to Senator Packwood saying: "Don't worry about lumber, Bob, we'll fix it".
Don't worry about timber.

That's right, don't worry about timber. We should recall the letter of May 8 from the President to Mr. Packwood of the Senate Finance Committee indicating that they would try the bilateral talks process, giving us a full week to try the entire envoy process. How marvellous to have a full week in order to negotiate for the largest singly-traded bilateral commodity between Canada and the United States, a

May 27, 1986
Supply
$25-billion industry thrown to the rocks. The President went on to say, "or unilateral trade action will be taken". It has now been taken and the Prime Minister had better wake up to what is going on.
I hear the Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister, the Premier of B.C. and others talking about putting some kind of fund together to assist the shake and shingle workers who have in some cases already lost their jobs and in others are about to lose their jobs. Where will the shake and shingle market be diversified to? Will it be diversified to the Arctic? It will not be diversified into Japan, Great Britain or other areas of the United States. The fact is that there are some other stick-handlers in this game at whom we as Canadians had better take a close look.
The tile producers and asphalt shingle producers in the United States are a part of this action. As well, the Washington, Oregon, Idaho and northern California shake and shingle producers want our bolts and our cedar logs because they do not have enough raw product to maintain their own position in the market.
I would like to deal for a moment with market penetration because that is one of the hot issues being used by the Americans. They say that we have gone from a 50-50 relationship to a 75-25 relationship. The reason we have greater participation in their market is that we have spent new money on shake and shingle production in British Columbia. We have more raw product available to us. We have a more competitive production process so we may sell that product at $38 to $40 per square to the United States.
Let us deal with that argument head on. While the United States has taken almost 150 petitioning processes of one kind or another against Canadian products since the so-called free trade negotiations began, Canada has not taken a single one against the United States. We have not protected our potatoes, our fish and many other commodities adequately. The U.S. is winning part of the argument right now. The Americans know that because of the level of bank loans to some of the shake and shingle producers in B.C. those producers are going to need to at least move bolts or logs to the United States market, and that is of course exactly what those guys want.
I was pleased to hear what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) had to say on May 27. At that time he said that the Government will not permit the Canadian shake and shingle industry to be exported across the border. That view is supported by the shake and shingle industry coalition with which I met yesterday. That coalition has already written to the Province of B.C., and I assume that letter will soon be in the hands of the Prime Minister, taking the exact same position. The shake and shingle workers do not want those 4,000 shake and shingle jobs in B.C. simply exported across the border so the American shake and shingle mills can pick up our jobs.
We now know where Liberal Members stand. They do not think that this is enough of a bad-faith issue, a British
Columbia issue or a Canadian issue, to call for the suspension of the trade talks on this issue alone. They are opposed to any kind of countervailing action or any kind of retaliatory action, but they have given themselves all kinds of escape routes rather than hitting the nail on the head. If at the very beginning of bilateral negotiations, such as those into which we have entered, we find that we are being dealt with in bad faith, as we have now discovered, we have to change the rules of the game and get back to square one.
I think it is worth while for Canadians to know just exactly who in the United States and who in Canada is interested in pushing for free trade talks. Since last September when the Prime Minister announced this initiative, I have never been stopped on the streets by anyone saying: "Jim, I want you to get in there and fight for these trade talks, they are going to get me a job". Do you know who in Canada is fighting for free trade? Do you know who is leaning on Simon Reisman and the Prime Minister? One simply need totter down to Bay Street and see who is going back and forth to Mr. Reisman's office, the $78,000-per-day operation, in their limousines. It is the big-seven families; the Bronfmans, the Reichmanns, Power Corporation, Conrad Black and Brascan. It is the big integrated operations that can move capital and branch plants easily back and forth across the border.
Who is for free trade in the United States? I should like to refer to the second page of Mr. Yeutter's evidence before the United States Senate Finance Committee. He referred to those U.S. industries which were most interested in seeing high Canadian tariffs eliminated-furniture, telecommunications equipment, home appliances, cosmetics, electronics, paper products, recreational boats, aluminum products, wall coverings, and leather. Then he pointed out that U.S. beer and wine interests wanted a good crack at the Canadian market, as well as poultry, eggs, dairy products, meat, and so on. There is the pressure.
How can we get a President and an administration that acted in bad faith during a process such as this to back off? How can we do it? I do not think it is by taking retaliatory measures against Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and California. I do not think that will assist at all. As I said earlier, it will pound in the last of the nails. It will also ensure that Secretary of Commerce Baldrige, on June 2, proceeds with the countervail action against Canadian softwood lumber.
The Leader of the Opposition said that it was just a shot across the bow of the Canadian lumber industry. My colleague reminded me that it was a direct hit, midships at the water line, for the shake and shingle industry. As it sinks, so too do our efforts in relation to the lumber issue. Contrary to what the previous speaker said, we know that case law has changed in the United States. Anyone in Canada interested in the forest industry who has not read the countervailing position, or the case law in the carbon black case from Mexico, had better read it pretty damn quick. If Secretary of Commerce Baldrige
May 27, 1986

and the President decide to proceed against the Canadian forest industry per se, we are in real trouble.
Backing that up, of course, is the fact that there is no longer 300 "Goosey-Lucy" Bills in the U.S. Congress. They have been amalgamated into one Bill, the Gibbons omnibus trade Bill, which is 485 pages long.
Let us think of the timing of this so-called great friend of Canada, President Reagan. Last Wednesday night that Bill went through with the support of the Democrats and the Republicans on a vote of 295 to 115, and it is before the United States Senate today. If it goes through this week, which is what is expected, as we learned in the forestry committee last Thursday, a countervailing duty could be brought against Canadian softwood products generically from coast to coast by July 4.
Let us think of the timing. In the same week the so-called free trade talks opened, a 35 per cent duty was imposed on B.C. shakes and shingles. Also in that same week there was the 295 to 115 vote on a 485-page Bill almost entirely directed against Canada. Let us think about exactly what they are after. It will affect the aluminum industry because its resource subsidy section goes after our entire resource base. It goes after 80 per cent of our trade with the United States. However, we talk about free trade, good faith, and trusting the President and the U.S. administration!
What has happened is that our new Government has not understood the politics of the issue and the depth of protectionism in the United States. I must say to my friends in the Liberal Party that I have been attending meetings continuously during the past year and I cannot recall a single occasion when any member of the Liberal Party came to those meetings. The motion before us is really a "Johnny-come-lately" motion. It is saying that suddenly the forest industry in Canada, the shake and shingle industry, is one of their most important concerns.
Cheap shots.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Yes, cheap shots.

Mr. Speaker, they want to deny it, but anyone can look at the record of who has attended the meetings of the forestry committee or who has attended the meetings in Vancouver with members of the U.S. subcommittee on trade and other such meetings. Anyone can find out that they are very much a "Johnny-come-lately" on this issue.
Let us deal for a moment with what is happening to the shake and shingle industry, and then I will return to protectionism. There will be a 35 per cent duty for 2.5 years. The coalition members made clear that almost none of them could survive in that 95 per cent of their product went into the U.S. market. Thereafter it will be 20 per cent for two years and 8 per cent for the six months following, if the U.S. industry still needs it.

The big difference is that this is a 201 ruling and 332 is the big one at which we are now looking. Between now and next Tuesday, when Secretary of Commerce Baldrige will make his determination on whether or not to proceed, we should take the strongest possible action we can. We started well last Friday with the unanimous motion of the House, and I think the U.S. Congress and President Reagan will have heard about it. We should suspend those comprehensive talks right now and say: "No more of this bad faith; you promised a clean launch and you did not deliver".
Perhaps the Prime Minister thinks that we can sacrifice those 4,000 jobs. Almost all of them, or a good healthy chunk of them, are in Mission-Port Moody. Some are in my constituency on the Queen Charlottes and in the northwest, but most of them are between Hope and Vancouver and on Vancouver Island.
Perhaps that industry will be sacrificed. Perhaps the Prime Minister and the Premier of British Columbia will say that they will put together a package to save those workers' jobs or whatever. Those workers know that that is not possible. There is not a market into which to diversify; there is not another readily accessible product. That kind of approach would be used simply to calm the concerns of Canadians generally, so that the Government can say it took action, that it assisted shake and shingle operators, and that they do not need to worry.
I should like to refer to the figures which were quoted by the previous speaker. They were given to us by the coalition yesterday. They are staggering. They indicate 4,000 jobs and a total of $344 million in relation to payroll, raw material, transportation, and supplies, as well as another 20,000 jobs indirectly and hundreds of millions of dollars. It went on to point out that the entire industry had been reduced from approximately seven million squares in 1977 down to four million squares in 1985, and that the majority of the loss was in the traditional marketing states of California and Texas. That is where the big move is on in terms of tile and asphalt shingles.
Also the coalition pointed out something which is key to evaluating the issue. It pointed out that it was important to note that the existing United States industry was not dead and that the portion which did not survive was not killed by Canadian production. It was killed as a result of loss of market, lack of economical raw material, and failure to automate. Also it pointed out that every Canadian firm which did not automate and adjust to markets has been removed from production as well during the same period of time.
In terms of existing inventories, the coalition pointed out that the 35 per cent tariff would add $40 million to the cost of existing inventories of raw materials and manufactured goods which cannot be processed and shipped prior to June 6. Not only is a $250 million industry at risk, also at risk are their inventories and the 20,000 associated indirect jobs, most of which are in the Fraser Valley. The Government has a responsibility not to ballyhoo and talk tough.

I should like to refer to a question I put to the Prime Minister on May 21. In part my question was:
I think he is aware that on May 8, President Reagan wrote a letter to Senator Packwood regarding Canadian softwood lumber in which he stated: "-I intend to press for an expedited resolution to this problem independent of comprehensive negotiations."
I am sure the Prime Minister is aware that President Reagan controls the acceptance or rejection of the countervailing action through Secretary of Commerce Baldrige. Has the Prime Minister himself, through his office, by phone, or by letter, contacted President Reagan and asked that this countervailing action be stopped?
The Prime Minister did not do what I suggested. He went on to say:
Mr. Speaker, no. I think I responded to that question yesterday. We are satisfied that the mechanisms in place are designed not only to eliminate problems but to create a climate of confidence within which these problems can be resolved. That is exactly what we are trying to do-not by yelling at the problems, not by denigrating anyone, but by sitting down in a reasonable, positive, and strong way to resolve these problems on behalf of Canadians.
That was six days ago. On Friday the Prime Minister decided it was time to yell at the President. That is his initiative. We will discover over the course of this debate and over the next couple of days what will be the personality of the Prime Minister and his Government and whether they will retaliate. If so, that will finish the shake and shingle industry. If they offer some kind of $500,000 adjustment program through FLIP, LEAP, JET, FLOP or whatever, it will be a total failure. They should take the constructive action which is absolutely necessary in this kind of relation and dialogue with the United States, our largest trading partner, with $130 billion last year-the largest bilateral trade in the world. Our largest single industry is now at risk. One Canadian in ten or one million people are at risk. We have just lost 4,000 jobs. That was a dead hit by the President at midships, and that ship is going down.
I want to hear from the Government side whether or not the Government is prepared to take the kind of bold Canadian initiatives upon which this country was founded, which is to say to the United States: "You cheated at cards and you are not going to get away with it. We are suspending the free trade talks today."

Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with everything the Hon. Member put forward this morning, but he did put forward some things that are of great concern to all of us. As he pointed out, the newly concerned individual from the Liberal Party, the right hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) has just arrived on the scene now that it is a national issue. It is important to note the answer he gave with regard to the exportation of logs and bolts. He said: "We will leave that for another day". What he is leaving for another day is possibly the exportation of jobs in Mission-Port Moody and jobs for Canadians right across the country. I would like the Hon. Member to give me his reaction to that. I am quite certain from the Member's speech that his concern is also the
same concern as ours, even though the Official Opposition has decided to put it off for another day.
When the Hon. Member spoke of the penetration of the market I think he left a few questions unanswered. He quite rightly depicted the American industry and what is happening in the United States, but he failed to point out that the amount of shakes and shingles used has decreased. We basically maintain our level of production and shipments to the United States but the U.S. has lost its portion, and that is quite important. This has been a declining market, but inasmuch as it is a declining market I just wanted to set the record straight on it.
The Member said we should suspend the free trade talks, but the solution to this problem lies in free trade because that is what is in jeopardy. Will the Hon. Member comment further on this? It appears he wants to cut off his nose to spite his face. In spite of this Draconian action taken by the President of the U.S.-it may be unethical but I do not believe it is illegal because laws exist under which the Americans can take this action-I still feel that the free trade negotiations have to be addressed in a more responsible manner. I would like the Hon. Member to reply to the logs and bolts issue which is so important to jobs in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to respond to the Hon. Member's point. It is clear that the Liberals really do not know where they are at on a lot of these issues. The Hon. Member, I believe, was the one who put the question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make sure that the Government's position stayed solid and that there would not be the export of logs and bolts. I am sure the Hon. Member is also aware of the study just released from the University of British Columbia produced by Michael Margolick and Russell Uhler. This study was funded by the Canadian Forest Service. It points out that by lifting the restrictions on log exports, which would include cedar logs, not directly bolts, there would be a short-term increase of $40 million a year to the log exporters but a direct loss of 3,200 jobs in the wood processing industry. Part of this is the desire by some in the United States who are extremely short of raw product-and here I am talking about the states of Washington, Oregon and Idaho-who need bolts and raw logs because they simply cannot get them in their own areas. They would very much like to see exported logs go down in price and domestic logs go up in price, because they would be getting firesale prices on cedar throughout that whole area. Not only would the industry be benefiting from the 35 per cent duty placed against our producers but it would be getting firesale product. Anyone who applies any logic to that would realize that that would immediately provide for the movement of those 4,000 jobs, or perhaps more, directly across the border.
As far as the second point made by the Hon. Member regarding market penetration is concerned, I pointed out that the coalition reminded me that our participation has been reduced from seven million squares in 1977 to four million squares in 1985. The market has constricted massively because
May 27, 1986

of the penetration of competing products, such as tile and asphalt.
To take this kind of Draconian action, to use the Hon. Member's words "unethical action", requires the strongest kind of response, and here I come directly to the point made by the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain). Should this country continue this so-called free trade process at this time? Again I come back to the analogy of playing cards for the first time. Whether you are a dealer or a player and you catch someone cheating, what do you do? Are you going to punish someone else because someone cheats?
We were given a country to country guarantee that there would be a clean launch. The Senate Finance Committee got tied up and we ended up with a 10-10 vote. Some special offers were made and are now being delivered to Senator Packwood and other Republican lumber state Senators. It is simply a question of whether you are prepared to continue dealing with someone who has cheated in the opening days of a process. That is what this is. You can call it unethical, you can call it bizarre, as the Prime Minister does. You can throw out all kinds of other language, but you have to withdraw from a process and evaluate internally within your own bureaucracy and political system and not allow the Americans to do something? The pressure will come very quickly, as it did on generic drugs and other things. There will be enormous pressure on the President. That 35 per cent duty would be withdrawn by next Tuesday, I can guarantee you, if we suspended those talks today, Mr. Speaker. I can absolutely guarantee that. The pressure on the White House from those who want to negotiate is far bigger than this. There is $130 billion in trade on the table to be negotiated on an annual basis. To worry because there is legislation in the U.S. Congress is one thing, but to say what is being done unilaterally and politically on a whim to apply this kind of duty means you have to call the cheater at the game.

Mr. Speaker, I honestly believe that the Hon. Member tried to leave the impression that the Prime Minister was not aware of this issue. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, as one who meets with the Prime Minister on a weekly basis and who chairs the national caucus, that this issue has been monitored from the day, that it arose on the scene in the U.S. and it has been an ongoing issue under discussion in our caucus. It is an issue with which the P.M. is totally current. He knows every aspect of it. We have kept the Prime Minister involved. The shock and the dismay the Prime Minister showed here last week was absolutely sincere.
Lies.

The Hon. Member aptly tried to present the fact that we were asleep at the switch. We were not. He knows that because I have been speaking with him on an ongoing basis. I know the Hon. Member has knowledge in this area. We have tried to work together. I want to let the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) know that the Prime

Minister knew everything about the issue. The Prime Minister knows more about shakes and shingles than many Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Member puts some interesting information on the record. But I think he knows that this information has been put forward a number of times by myself, by members of the forest industry and by our own embassy people in Washington. I am convinced some of them are about to go down the tube, partly in relation to this issue, in a desire to shoot the messenger.
The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody was in Washington at the same time I was last year, and he heard what the Americans had to say. He knows they wanted far more resources, that they wanted to be able to get information out, not just to the national home builders, or to other groups in the U.S., but to get information out to the two million Americans who go to work everyday and get their pay packets from producing commodities for the Canadian market. We missed. I am saying this as a country. I am not going to lay all the blame on the Prime Minister , but his responsible Cabinet members, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were not listening to our embassy in Washington. They were not listening to the Canadian forest industry.
After skating close to the edge the shake and shingle industry has now fallen over the edge. Next Tuesday will be the telling day in Canadian history. If Secretary of Commerce Baldridge says that he is going ahead with Bill 332 we will lose a million jobs in Canada. We lost 4,000 jobs last week and a million will be on the table next week. We have been asleep at the switch. We have not done our job in dealing with the grass roots political issue in the United States. Fifty per cent of the wood in Georgia, the largest softwood producing state in the United States, is from British Columbia.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond on behalf of the Government to the opening remarks of the two Opposition Parties. It is perhaps timely that I intervene because I am afraid that the huffing and puffing which has been going on may blow the House down and we would not want that to happen.
I welcome this debate because it has forced the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to give an indication of the position of the Liberal Party with regard to the efforts which the Government has initiated to develop a more predictable and enhanced trade relationship with our neighbour to the south. The Hon. Member said that he spoke for an hour a month ago. At a future date to be determined they will try to refine their position further.
Their position in the first speech was that the timing is bad because we presently have a trade surplus with the United States and because they are holding mid-term elections. In the United States there is a presidential election every four years

May 27, 1986
Supply
and a mid-term election every two years. It is perhaps because of that Liberal logic that we have the problems which we are presently facing.
The timing is never good to make tough decisions, particularly when dealing with the most important trade relationship between any two countries in the world. The timing to take courageous decisions is never good. We know that the Liberal position is to stay away from the trade talks because the timing is bad. I would like the Liberals to tell us when the timing will be good. Perhaps that is why we have seen no action from them other than to antagonize the most important friends that we have had in the last 20 years, which have now put us in this position.
I would like the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) to tell me whose jack-in-the-box he is today. Is he the jack-in-the-box of Bob White who says that we should get away from any trade talks? He says that he is okay because he has the Auto Pact and has told the Americans where to get off. However, the last word has not been spoken on that. Or, is he the jack-in-the-box of Jack Munro in B.C. who will be affected by this situation? Has the Member asked Jack Munro how he feels about getting more secure access for our lumber in the United States? Who is he defending in the House today?
We know their position. Under no circumstances do they want enhanced and more secure trade with the United States. They say: "To hell with our $112 billion of exports to the United States". I would like the Member to tell me where we will find markets to replace the market in the United States. You cannot always dump on your friends, call them cheaters and crooks, and then say that you did not really mean it and ask them to buy your products. That is NDP logic. They have nothing and want to share it with everyone.
The Government needs no urging from Members opposite to take all the appropriate actions to defend our trade interests in the United States or in any other market in the world. While members of the Opposition are only now waking up to the fact that the B.C. shake and shingle producers are vulnerable to protectionist trade actions in the United States, the Government has been taking action. Has the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, my friend who represents a riding in British Columbia, asked a single question in the House over the last eight months on this issue?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I say "no". We have taken action to defend our shake and shingle exports to the United States and to negotiate better rules to ensure that tariff and non-tariff barriers do not impede our exports to the United States. We have negotiated rules to protect Canadian exports, not only of shingles and shakes, but of lumber, hogs, steel, fish, potatoes, uranium and a whole range of other Canadian exports that are the subject of protectionist measures in the United States.
More than eight months have passed since the United States shake and shingle producers petitioned their Government for
import relief under U.S. trade remedy legislation. We were aware of this situation eight months ago and we acted. We did not act only in response to a letter of May 7 from the Premier of the Province of British Columbia. We have been working on this issue for the last eight months. It is more than two months since the United States International Trade Commission recommended that the President impose a punitive tariff on imports of red cedar shakes and shingles. For over eight months the Government has been in the trenches working with the Canadian industry to defend our access to the United States market for shakes and shingles.
One might well ask where the Opposition was. Why have we not heard before of their new-found concern for protection of jobs which were at risk in the shake and shingles industry? The Government assisted the industry in developing the argument we presented to the U.S. International Trade Commission. I can assure the House that the Canadian Government's opposition to the International Trade Commission's recommendation was put to the U.S. Government forcefully and on many occasions.
The punitive tariff announced by President Reagan on May 22, which is to take effect on June 6, is not in our view an appropriate remedy to address the problems of the U.S. shake and shingle industry. They are not just destroying the Canadian industry, but their own industry as well. If they think that the British Columbia Government, or indeed the Canadian Government, would be inclined to send them the raw materials to revive their own industry, they will have to think again. The problems with the United States industry, are long-term and relate primarily to a shortage of domestic raw materials and competition from alternative products. Perhaps the exchange rate has become a problem for that industry as it has for other industries.
Western red cedar is for all practical purposes a nonrenewable resource. The U.S. supply of old growth western red cedar, the raw material used to make red cedar shingles and shakes, is dwindling very rapidly. The United States International Trade Commission's report on the investigation estimated that the supply of old growth cedar in the United States would be totally depleted within 20 years. Some experts say that that will happen in an even shorter time frame.
Intense competition from other substitutable products such as asphalt tiles is reducing the shingle and shake market and will prevent significant price increases even if the very high tariff that has been imposed stays in effect. Changes in building and fire codes in many jurisdictions effectively prohibit the use of untreated wood shingles and shakes. In fact, as the Hon. Member for Skeena pointed out, our own shipments to the United States have been drastically reduced. Builders, architects and homeowners are switching to substitute products because of growing concerns about fire safety issues. The substitute products have a number of advantages over traditional wood materials, such as superior warranties, and are highly price-competitive with wood shingles and shakes.
May 27, 1986

For all of these reasons we argued forcefully in all of our consultations and representaions that tariffs or quotas would not address the fundamental problems of U.S. producers. At the same time U.S. border measures would create great hardship for those Canadians whose livelihood depends on our bilateral trade in these products. No Member of this House knows better than I the hardship which these protectionist measures will generate for the workers in this industry and their communities, primarily in British Columbia. Some 4,000 Canadians, as has been pointed out, are employed in the production of shingles and shakes. Over 90 per cent of the industry's production is exported to the United States. It is difficult to argue the precise impact of these protectionist measures on current production and trade levels. Estimates range from 10 to 40 per cent reduction. Only time will tell, but it is most certainly a cause for serious concern.
As Members of this House are aware, the Canadian Government's response to this protectionist trade action by the United States President has been swift and vigorous. The Government's objections have been conveyed directly to the president and to Secretary of State Schultz by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), as well as in a diplomatic note protesting the U.S. action in the strongest terms. The note is public and I am sure I do not have to read it out for Hon. Members.
I can assure the Member's opposite that the United States authorities are well aware of the resolution unanimously adopted by this House last Friday. Let there be no doubt also that the Government now has under active consideration a range of options which might constitute an appropriate response in the event the U.S. Government is not prepared to rescind these tariffs or offer acceptable compensation. Included in the range of options available to the Government would be some direct assistance for the British Columbia producers, who stand to be most seriously affected. My colleagues, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) will have this issue high on their agenda in meetings later on this week with their U.S. counterparts, Secretary of State Schultz and Ambassador Yeutter, the United States trade representative.
I would contend that the resolution we are debating today is shortsighted and unrealistic. When we speak of protectionism and trade and free trade we speak of markets. It was Adam Smith who said 200 years ago that a nation's ability to grow and expand economically in an industrial sense depends as much on its ability to consume as it does on its ability to produce. Canada is more dependent on trade with other countries than is any other nation in the world. Protectionism works in favour of those countries which have something to protect in terms of markets. We have a very limited market and, therefore, enhanced trade has to be our battle cry.
Supply
If the Opposition thinks that the Americans came to us begging to get into these enhanced trade talks they are wrong. It is in our interests to develop more secure and better access to foreign markets wherever they are, whether they are in the United States, in the new emerging Asian markets or in the European countries.
We are the only nation among the important industrial nations that does not have unimpeded and secure access to a market in excess of a hundred million people. We are the only outsiders in the industrial world. Unless we correct this problem and find more secure, predictable access to a market which meets a certain economy of scale we shall fade away as an industrial nation into obscurity and insignificance.
The Opposition is asking us to hold the trade negotiations hostage to specific trade irritants, when the trade negotiations are so clearly in our best interests. These negotiations, if successful, could reduce our vulnerability to actions like the tariff increase on shakes and shingles. It is unrealistic because it would be neither appropriate nor possible for either Government to implement some sort of standstill with respect to actions which are not discretionary under the existing trade laws.
Surely the Opposition would not suggest that Canadian producers could be unilaterally denied their right to seek relief from injury in case of dumping or subsidized imports while the trade negotiations are underway. Is the Opposition aware that the Ontario corn producers have requested a countervail investigation against subsidized corn imported from the United States? Canadian agricultural producers are acutely aware of the massive subsidies made available to the United States farmer in the new Farm Bill.
There are, of course, discretionary decisions. The action on shakes and shingles was a discretionary decision by President Reagan. We do not like it and we are dismayed by the decision. We find it impossible to understand. It makes no economic sense. It destroys their own industry as well. It is bad trade policy, and it is a breach of a political commitment not to introduce new barriers to cross-border trade. We would hope that this is an isolated case, an aberration that will not be repeated while trade negotiations are underway.
No case could illustrate better that the current international trade rules do not provide the certainty and security of access to the U.S. market which Canadians producers need to plan their future and to improve their investment position. We are all well aware that countervailing duty actions are a serious threat to our access to the United States. Over our heads still hangs this dark cloud on softwood lumber. The GATT permits the application of countervailing duties in situations where subsidized imports are found to be injurious to domestic producers. The GATT rules on subsidies and countervailing duties do not provide affected exporters with rights to compensation or retaliation except as a last resort flowing from recourse to GATT dispute settlement procedures.

In the case of the new countervailing duty petition on lumber, Members of this House are well aware of the Government's strongly held view that initiation of a new investigation cannot be justified. Neither the material facts nor U.S. law have changed since Canadian lumber producers were found by the Commerce Department in 1983 not to be benefiting from countervailing subsidies. The Americans do not understand our system, they are comparing it with theirs.
We in British Columbia, as the Hon. Member from Skeena knows, have to put in place a management regime which is consistent and conducive to the problems that we have in British Columbia. We still have massive virgin stands of timber which are becoming over mature and rotting away. The Hon. Member from Skeena and his friends think that the trees actually grow to heaven if you leave them standing long enough. A tree is a living thing, it has a life span, and when that life span is complete it is of no use to a shingle and shake producer or to a lumber producer, it dies. We in Canada and British Columbia must have a different management regime than what they have in the southern United States where they are dealing with fourth and fifth generation timber.
We have made plain to the Americans our intention to invoke GATT dispute settlement procedures in the event a new investigation is initiated. Our ambassador in Geneva was instructed to make a statement on May 22 to the GATT council. I have the statement here; I will not delay the House by reading it into the record, but I certainly would be prepared to table it. We have made a very strong case pointing out all the facts I have mentioned.
There is no doubt that protectionist pressures in the United States are strong and they are growing. Each of these investigations or tariffs, or trade restrictive actions, no matter what the outcome, takes its toll, both in legal expenses to fight U.S. protectionism and immeasureable damage to the Canadian investment climate.
Let me reiterate for the benefit of the Members opposite that the resolution we are debating is shortsighted. Trade negotiations are in Canada's interests. Last week's events are but one example of the shortcomings in the current contractual rules. The status quo is not good enough. We need a better set of rules for the conduct of our trade and economic relations with the United States.
The existing rules can be improved only through negotiations. There are two avenues along which negotiations can take place. One is bilateral, with our principal trading partner. The other is multilateral, under the GATT. The Government is pursuing both avenues.
Finally, let me reiterate for the benefit of those opposite that the Government recognizes the hardship and personal economic dislocation that could result from the 35 per cent tariff on cedar shakes and shingles in British Columbia and similar threats to our Canadian access to U.S. markets with
other products. The Government has launched negotiations aimed at a better contractual basis for the conduct of our trade relations with the United States. If members of the Opposition are genuine in their concern for Canadian cedar shake and shingle producers, they will lend their support to our important initiatives and endeavours.

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of questions for the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle). I hope he will attempt to respond to my question about the shake and shingle and lumber issue.
The Minister is very much aware that we have had absolute unrestricted, unfettered, tariff-free trade with the United States in softwood lumber and shakes and shingles for half a century. I hope the Minister has not been permeated by what I consider to be incredible lunacy and naivety on the part of the Government. Will the Minister explain why he kept avoiding the history of the shake and shingle issue when we are involved in these trade negotiations? Can he explain this unilateral action which has been taken after a tie vote at the Internan-tional Trade Commission, including the chair having voted against applying any kind of restrictive duty on Canadian shakes and shingles? Why does the Minister believe that these negotiations will help after half a century of unrestricted free trade? What can be freer than free?
The U.S. is going after this particular industry. Will the Minister tell me how this issue will be resolved in the negotiations between Peter Murphy and Simon Reisman? The Minister knows full well that this issue will not be on the table. If we do not ensure that these duties are removed totally right now, they will be levied against the industry for five years.
Will the Minister explain what is freer than free trade and tell us whether the Senate is likely to give up such countervail powers? It has made it clear that it will not.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member has never heard it said that nothing endures more than change. The fact that we have had unimpeded and unfettered access to the U.S. for our lumber does not mean that this will always be the case. In fact, we now know that it is not the case.
This countervailing duty action began long before we started our negotiations on the enhanced trade issue.
No. Four months after.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Perhaps the countervail duties started as a result of a prolonged problem facing the United States in terms of balancing its trade, not only with Canada but with other parts of the world due to currency problems. In the last 10 or 15 years Canadians have had a very distinct advantage over American producers as a result of the spread in the currency exchange, which also allowed us to become most efficient and make great efficiency gains in our mills. The Americans are saying that enough is enough and that is why these actions have come about.
May 27, 1986

Previous governments should have had our foresight to see this and recognize the value of our resource industries. If they had secured that access with some formal relationship, perhaps similar to the Auto Pact, and built on the strengths of our regions as we intend to do, we would have an arrangement to protect that pillar of our economy in Canada. Now we must operate after the fact and simply because there has always been that free trade does not mean it will continue forever. Changes are imminent and we have to react in the best way possible.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister referred to the importance of securing that American market for Canadians. I believe that certain forms of retaliatory action have begun, as mentioned by other Members. For instance, I am receiving letters from my constituency describing how some constituents will not buy American orange juice. The fact that I am receiving these letters from British Columbia in three days may be a miracle in itself, but the fact is that people are reacting to this issue already. In Nanaimo Harbour, there was consideration given to buying a large fleet of American forklift trucks but now they are contemplating buying them elsewhere.
Will the Minister agree that trying to save one job through a tariff measure has the effect of losing three or four jobs? Will he comment on some of the remarks of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he said that the Americans were actually aiming at the Japanese with their $50 billion trade surplus but somehow Canada has become involved with our $20 billion surplus? Is the Leader of the Opposition accurate in saying that if we had not begun free trade talks this tariff would not have come about?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will answer the last question first. Everyone knows that this problem has existed throughout the 1970s but is compounding and becoming very serious. The United States must find a way to come to grips with their problems. They believe they should not be held to ransom by the rest of the world simply because they have decided to play a major role in correcting some of the serious imbalances with Third World debt and those greater issues which are involved. This means that protectionist measures through their more direct system of democracy are the order of the day in the United States. The Hon. Member referred to the many Bills presently before Congress.
We believe that we should have developed a special relationship between our two countries ten years ago because of the great dependence on each other for this trade. Neither we nor the Americans can afford to enter into a trade war because this involves winners and losers. Since we have the most to lose, it does not make sense for us to even mention the word. That does not mean that we should play dead every time a measure is directed against us. We should be strong in our resolve to tell the Americans that if they had made the same decision as we made some years ago, to modernize our industries, to become more competitive, and to react better
